API\tissue-73-9b73254076aa\tMERGED\t2026-11-20T08:59:35Z\n   231 docs/VISION.md\n   581 docs/ROADMAP.md\n   641 docs/CONTRIBUTING.md\n  1453 total\n# Vision\n\nvoice-simulator is a physical model of the human voice that works in both\ndirections:\n\n```\ntext in a language  ->  IPA  ->  articulation  ->  sound      (speaking)\ntext in a language  <-  IPA  <-  articulation  <-  sound      (listening)\n```\n\nSpeaking simulates the air in a human head. Listening runs the same simulation\nin reverse: it finds the head, the voice and the movements that would have\nproduced the sound it hears, and reads the speech off those movements. Nothing\nis recorded and nothing is learned by a neural network. The project is in the\npublic domain and is a gift to everyone.\n\nThis document is the single statement of where the project is going. It is\nupdated by every pull request that changes the direction; the history is at the\nend. The step-by-step plan that implements it is [ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md).\n\n## Principles\n\nThese are rules, not preferences. A change that breaks one of them is not\nmerged.\n\n1. **Physics and mathematics only.** Sound comes from simulated air, folds,\n   walls and turbulence. Recognition comes from inverting that simulation.\n   No neural network is used anywhere: not in the library, not in the app,\n   not in the tests and not in the tools that build the data tables. No\n   recorded speech is played back or concatenated. The exact boundary is in\n   [What counts as a neural network](#what-counts-as-a-neural-network).\n2. **One model, two directions.** Speaking and listening share the same head,\n   the same articulation channels, the same IPA inventory and the same\n   prosody rules. A feature is finished when it works both ways: whatever the\n   simulator can say, it can recognise, and every mode of speech it detects, it\n   can produce.\n3. **Always through IPA.** Text is never mapped to sound directly, and sound\n   is never mapped to text directly. Speaking is text in a language → IPA →\n   audio. Listening is audio → IPA → the language, or the mix of languages,\n   → text. IPA with its tone, stress, length and voice-quality marks is the\n   interchange format between every stage and between the two directions.\n4. **The highest quality the device can afford, never silence.** The most\n   accurate simulation is the reference. Every device gets the most detailed\n   variant it can run in real time, measured on that device in the background,\n   and the quality steps down while speaking the moment the device falls\n   behind. The same holds for listening.\n5. **It works at the bottom too.** Synthesis, recognition and voice copying\n   all work at the lowest settings: narrow-band audio, the cheapest solver, one\n   CPU core. More cores, a GPU and higher settings make it better, never make\n   it possible.\n6. **Everything that changes a voice is a parameter.** Anatomy, the vocal\n   folds, breathing, articulation habits, accent and expression are numbers\n   with physical units, documented ranges and sources. A voice is a set of\n   those numbers, so it can be edited, saved, copied from a recording and\n   compared.\n7. **Measured against real speech.** Claims of quality are backed by numbers\n   computed on public recordings of real people with transcripts, by\n   algorithms that are themselves free of neural networks, and by listening\n   tests with people. A claim that was not measured is written as a goal.\n8. **Reproducible.** The same input, seed and settings give the same samples\n   on every runtime. Results of experiments are committed with the script\n   that produced them.\n9. **Public domain.** The code is released under the Unlicense. Data that is\n   committed to the repository is public domain or CC0. Dependencies have\n   permissive licences. Anything else is fetched at test time and never\n   redistributed.\n\n## What the system does when the vision is reached\n\n### Speaking\n\n- Reads text in every supported language, normalises it, converts it to IPA\n  and speaks it with a voice that people cannot tell from a recording of a\n  person in a blind listening test. That is the meaning of \"state of the art\"\n  here, and it is a goal, not a current claim.\n- Speaks in every common mode of speech: statements, all kinds of questions,\n  exclamations, commands, lists and asides; lexical tones and pitch accents;\n  word stress and rhythm; regional and foreign accents; soft, normal, loud and\n  shouted speech with gradual changes of loudness; whisper, breathy, creaky,\n  pressed and falsetto voice; emotions and attitudes; breaths, laughter, sighs\n  and hesitations.\n- Simulates the voice source as a physical system (vocal folds driven by lung\n  pressure, coupled to the air below and above them), the turbulence at\n  constrictions, the losses in the walls and the radiation from the mouth and\n  nose, in 1D for speed and in full 3D for accuracy.\n- Highlights every syllable in the text at the moment it is spoken.\n\n### Listening\n\n- Takes a recording or a live microphone and returns IPA with times, the\n  language or languages spoken, and the text, using the simulation in reverse.\n- Recognises the same modes of speech that it can produce and writes them\n  down with the same marks: tones, stress, sentence type, loudness, whisper\n  and other voice qualities, emotion.\n- Highlights every syllable as it is recognised.\n\n### Copying a voice\n\n- Works in several passes that feed each other. The first pass fits the\n  configuration of the voice: the size and shape of the head, the vocal folds,\n  the habits of articulation. The second pass inverts the simulation with\n  that configuration to recover the movements and the phonemes. As the person\n  keeps speaking both estimates are refined until they are stable. From then\n  on the system holds a voice it can speak with and a recogniser tuned to that\n  speaker, and it can follow what the person says.\n- Reproduces a real recording: the copy says the same words with the same\n  timing, melody and voice quality, close enough to be measured against the\n  original.\n\n### Running everywhere\n\n- The simulation core is written in Rust. In browsers it runs as WebAssembly\n  in a background worker and is the default engine; the same core runs natively\n  in the command line tool and the server. The JavaScript implementation stays\n  as the readable reference and as the fallback.\n- A short benchmark runs in the background when the page loads, without sound\n  and without blocking the interface, and decides the precision for this\n  device. While speaking, the quality follows the measured load and changes\n  without a click or a gap.\n- It uses all CPU cores when the platform allows it and works on one core\n  when it does not.\n- Expensive tests (full 3D renders, recognition of datasets, voice copying)\n  run in manually triggered GitHub Actions workflows; the tests that run on\n  every pull request stay fast.\n\n## What counts as a neural network\n\nNot allowed, in the product, the tests, the build tools and the continuous\nintegration:\n\n- Artificial neural networks of any kind and size (perceptrons, convolutional,\n  recurrent, transformer and diffusion models), whether trained by this project\n  or downloaded.\n- Libraries whose purpose is to run or train them.\n- Scoring our output with neural models (for example neural speech recognisers\n  or neural quality predictors).\n\nAllowed:\n\n- Physical simulation and its inversion.\n- Closed-form mathematics and signal processing: Fourier and linear-prediction\n  analysis, filters, cepstra, autocorrelation.\n- Search and optimisation: dynamic programming, Viterbi decoding, least\n  squares, gradient descent on the parameters of the physical model,\n  derivative-free and evolutionary optimisers, Kalman and particle filters.\n- Tables with a documented source: pronunciation dictionaries, measured\n  anatomical dimensions, vowel formants, and counts taken from public text or\n  recordings (for example how often one phoneme follows another). Every table\n  is small enough to read, is produced by a committed script and names its\n  data.\n- Calibrating the constants of the rules and of the physical model against\n  recordings by optimisation.\n\nNeural systems remain the yardstick. Their published scores are quoted, and\ntheir audio may be one of the samples in a listening test with people. They\nare never a component.\n\n## Where the project is today\n\nVersion 0.11 speaks; it does not listen yet.\n\n| Area               | Today                                                                                                      | Gap to the vision                                                                                                        |\n| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |\n| Languages          | English, Russian, Hindi and Mandarin Chinese to IPA, with text normalisation; four English accents         | Small dictionaries: wrong stress and wrong readings of words spelled alike; accents for English only                     |\n| Prosody            | Pauses, final pitch movements and lengthening from punctuation; lexical tones from start and end level     | No model of intonation per language, no focus or emphasis, tones lose their middle target, no expressive modes           |\n| Voice source       | Liljencrants-Fant pulse with tenseness, breathiness, jitter, shimmer, vibrato and a glottal chink          | No simulated vocal folds, no lung pressure, no whisper, creak or falsetto, no coupling of the source to the tract        |\n| Acoustics          | 1D waveguide in real time; sparse-voxel 3D FDTD (WebAssembly kernel, optional WebGPU) at 1 to 0.4 cm       | The 3D default is about 12 times slower than real time on a CPU; frequency-dependent losses and noise sources are simple |\n| Configuration      | 33 head and voice parameters, three presets                                                                | Folds, breathing, expression and articulation habits are not parameters yet                                              |\n| Performance        | JavaScript engine in a Web Worker, start-up benchmark, restart on a cheaper tier in the first 40-300 ms    | No Rust engine, one core only, no change of quality in the middle of an utterance, lowest tier is 22.05 kHz              |\n| Listening          | `analyzeVoice` measures pitch, formants, tilt, noise and rate; `matchVoice` fits six parameters            | No recognition of phonemes, language or text; voice matching was tested on synthetic recordings only                     |\n| Syllable highlight | While speaking, from the planned timeline                                                                  | Not for recognition                                                                                                      |\n| Evidence           | Formant checks against Hillenbrand et al. (1995) and Story (2008); anatomy checked against MRI and atlases | No test on recordings of running speech, no listening test                                                               |\n\nThe measurements behind this table, the full list of requirements and the\nresearch are in the case studies:\n[issue 1](case-studies/issue-1/README.md) (the prototype),\n[issue 5](case-studies/issue-5/README.md) (precision),\n[issue 9](case-studies/issue-9/README.md) (quality) and\n[issue 11](case-studies/issue-11/README.md) (this vision).\n\n## How quality is judged\n\n- **Speaking.** Distance between a synthesised sentence and a real recording\n  of the same sentence: spectral distortion, pitch and formant error, timing\n  of syllables. Intelligibility measured by people and by our own recogniser.\n  Naturalness measured by people in blind comparisons that include real\n  recordings and other synthesisers. The first measurement of the spectral,\n  pitch, formant and timing distances on the golden set is\n  [reports/baseline-quality.md](reports/baseline-quality.md); later work\n  compares itself with it (`scripts/quality-report.mjs --baseline`).\n- **Listening.** Phoneme, syllable, word and character error rates on public\n  recordings with transcripts, per language and per audio setting, including\n  the lowest one. Language identification accuracy, including mixed speech.\n- **Copying.** Error of the recovered parameters on synthetic recordings\n  where the truth is known, and distance between the copy and the original on\n  real recordings.\n- **Round trip.** What the simulator says, it must recognise: text → audio →\n  text returns the input in every language, mode and tier.\n- **Speed.** Real-time factor of every tier per device class, time to first\n  sound, and the cost of the load-time benchmark.\n\nEvery number is reported with the script, the data and the commit that\nproduced it.\n\n## Not goals\n\n- Neural text-to-speech or speech recognition, or wrapping existing engines.\n- Playing back, concatenating or morphing recorded speech.\n- Diagnosis or treatment of voice disorders. The simulator can model unusual\n  voices, but it is not a medical device.\n- Impersonating a real person without their consent. Voice copying exists to\n  let people use and study their own voices and public-domain recordings.\n\n## History of the vision\n\n| Issue                                                      | What it added                                                                                                                                                                                                       |\n| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| [#1](https://github.com/konard/voice-simulator/issues/1)   | A physical 3D voice simulator instead of a recording- or network-based one: text → IPA → articulation → waves in a low-poly head; four languages; library, command line, server and one app for every platform      |\n| [#5](https://github.com/konard/voice-simulator/issues/5)   | Precision everywhere: teeth, tongue and palate; microphone and room; every parameter that changes the sound; presets; copying a voice from a recording; audio formats; punctuation; accents; syllable highlighting  |\n| [#9](https://github.com/konard/voice-simulator/issues/9)   | Full 3D acoustics by default, quality chosen per device, female and child voices that sound right, anatomy checked against real data                                                                                |\n| [#11](https://github.com/konard/voice-simulator/issues/11) | State of the art without neural networks; the reverse direction (audio → IPA → language → text); multi-pass voice copying; Rust engine; quality that adapts while streaming; all modes of speech in both directions |\n\nOne recommendation of the issue 9 case study is withdrawn. It proposed to\nlearn the control of the articulators with a sequence model and to add a small\nneural residual to the output, and to score the result with neural recognisers\nand neural quality predictors. Issue 11 rules neural networks out. The gap that\nrecommendation addressed is real, namely that the control of the voice, its\nprosody and its source matter more than the acoustics of the tract. It is now\nclosed by rules and physical models whose constants are calibrated against\nreal recordings by optimisation, and it is measured by the methods in\n[How quality is judged](#how-quality-is-judged).\n# Contributing to js-ai-driven-development-pipeline-template\n\n## Development Workflow\n\nUse Node.js 24 with npm 10.9 or newer for development and release tooling.\nChangesets 3 requires a supported Node.js 22.11, 24, or 26+ runtime.\n\n1. **Fork the repository** and clone your fork\n2. **Create a feature branch**: `git checkout -b feature/my-feature`\n3. **Install dependencies**: `bun install` (or `npm install`)\n4. **Make your changes**\n5. **Run local checks**: `bun run check`\n6. **Create a changeset**: `bun run changeset`\n7. **Commit and push** (pre-commit hooks will run automatically)\n8. **Create a Pull Request**\n\n## Code Standards\n\n### File Size Limits\n\n**Maximum 1500 lines per file** (enforced via ESLint `max-lines` rule and CI `check-file-line-limits` job).\n\nThis benefits both AI and human developers by ensuring files remain readable and maintainable.\n\n### Formatting and Linting\n\nAll code must pass:\n\n```bash\n# Check formatting\nbun run format:check\n\n# Check linting\nbun run lint\n\n# Run all checks\nbun run check\n```\n\nThe pre-commit hook runs automatically, but you can also manually format and fix:\n\n```bash\n# Auto-fix formatting\nbun run format\n\n# Auto-fix lint issues\nbun run lint:fix\n```\n\n### Testing Requirements\n\nTests should:\n\n- Cover critical paths\n- Work across all runtimes (Node.js, Bun, Deno)\n- Use the [test-anywhere](https://github.com/link-foundation/test-anywhere) framework\n\n```bash\n# Run tests\nbun test --timeout 30000\nnpm test\ndeno test -A --parallel\n```\n\nTests that need more than about 10 seconds or a download do not belong in\n`tests/*.test.js`; put them into `tests/heavy/` (see \"Heavy checks\" below).\n\n### Heavy checks\n\nSlow tests (full 3D renders, quality reports against recordings, recognition\nof datasets, round trips, voice copying) live in `tests/heavy/` and are named\n`<suite>-<topic>.test.js`, where the suite is `quality`, `recognition`,\n`roundtrip`, `copy`, `performance`, `gpu` or `lexicon`. `npm test`, `bun test` and\n`deno test` never run them; [tests/heavy/README.md](../tests/heavy/README.md)\ndescribes the folder and its helpers.\n\nThey run in the workflow `Heavy checks`\n([.github/workflows/heavy.yml](../.github/workflows/heavy.yml)), which is only\nstarted by hand:\n\n- in the **Actions** tab: choose **Heavy checks**, then **Run workflow**, pick\n  the branch, the suite, optionally a `ref` (a branch or tag of this\n  repository, or a commit already on `main` or on the branch picked; empty\n  means the branch picked)\n  and a `limit` (largest number of items, such as utterances or files, that\n  each test may process; empty means no limit);\n- from the command line:\n\n  ```bash\n  gh workflow run heavy.yml -f suite=quality -f limit=5\n  # on another branch\n  gh workflow run heavy.yml --ref my-branch -f suite=performance\n  ```\n\nA run started on `main` writes to the cache scope of `main`, so\n[scripts/resolve-heavy-ref.sh](../scripts/resolve-heavy-ref.sh) refuses a\n`ref` that names anything else, such as a commit of a fork; to test a pull\nrequest from a fork, start the workflow on its branch after pushing that\nbranch here.\n\nThe run summary shows one row per test file with its result and wall time,\nfollowed by the reports the tests wrote; the reports are also uploaded as the\nartifact `heavy-<suite>-<run id>` and kept for 30 days. The step has a budget\nof 300 minutes (see [CI-TIMEOUT-BUDGETS.md](CI-TIMEOUT-BUDGETS.md)).\n\nLocally:\n\n```bash\nnpm run test:heavy -- --suite performance\nnpm run test:heavy -- --suite performance --limit 2 --out /tmp/heavy\n```\n\nReports go to `reports/heavy/` (`--out` changes the folder): every test writes\n`<name>.md` and `<name>.json`, and the runner writes `summary.md`. `reports/`\nis never committed. A report that should be kept is copied to `docs/reports/`\nby the issue that owns it.\n\n#### Round-trip recognition\n\nRun `npm run test:heavy -- --suite roundtrip` to measure synthetic speech\nrecognition on a fixed corpus of 80 sentences in English, Russian, Hindi and\nMandarin. The suite tests four presets across nine tiers and reports phone and\ntext errors, lexical tone and stress, syllable timing, language, punctuation,\nspeech modes and recognition speed. For a shorter run, append `--limit 2` to\ncap each language's sentence sample before testing its tiers and presets.\nThe full run produces the [round-trip report](reports/roundtrip.md).\n\n#### Performance tracking\n\n`tests/heavy/performance-tiers.test.js` (issue 31) times every audio tier\nexcept `reference` on the JavaScript and the Rust engine, on one core, and\nwrites `performance-tiers.json`. In CI, or locally with\n`PERFORMANCE_COMPARE=1`, its test `speed rules hold` compares the run with\n[docs/reports/performance-baseline.json](reports/performance-baseline.json)\nthrough [scripts/performance.mjs](../scripts/performance.mjs): a row more than\nthe tolerance (2.0, from the spread of five CI runs) slower than its baseline\nrow (scaled by a calibration loop, so a slower runner is forgiven), a missing\nrow, a Rust row slower than its\nJavaScript row, or a waveguide tier above half of real time fails the run. The\nsame script compares any two reports by hand:\n\n```bash\nnode scripts/performance.mjs compare reports/heavy/performance-tiers.json\nnode scripts/performance.mjs compare new.json --baseline old.json --tolerance 2\n```\n\nThe calibration loop does not follow every machine: a busy developer machine\nrenders slower than its calibration says, so a local comparison with the CI\nbaseline can fail with no change of code. Compare with a baseline of your own\nmachine instead:\n\n```bash\nnode scripts/performance.mjs baseline reports/heavy/performance-tiers.json --dir /tmp/mine\nPERFORMANCE_COMPARE=1 PERFORMANCE_BASELINE=/tmp/mine/performance-baseline.json \\\n  npm run test:heavy -- --suite performance\n```\n\nThe workflow never commits; the files in `docs/reports/` change only in a pull\nrequest, from the artifact of a green run of suite `performance`:\n\n- **Trend.** Every pull request that changes `src/acoustics/`, `src/engine/`\n  or `crates/`, and every minor release, adds its row to\n  [docs/reports/performance.md](reports/performance.md):\n  `node scripts/performance.mjs trend performance-tiers.json` (a second run of\n  the same commit replaces the first).\n- **Baseline.** Replace the baseline only for a wanted change of speed, and\n  give the reason in the pull request:\n  `node scripts/performance.mjs baseline performance-tiers.json`. A row with\n  the status `faster` is the hint that the baseline is out of date.\n\n#### Suite `gpu`\n\nThe files `gpu-*.test.js` run the WebGPU 3D solver, which Node.js and Bun\nlack, so the runner gives them, together with `tests/fdtd-gpu.test.js`, to\n`deno test -A --config deno.heavy.json` after the Node.js files. The suite\nneeds Deno on `PATH`; without it their rows in `summary.md` say\n`skipped (no Deno)`. `deno.heavy.json` has its own import of `test-anywhere`\nand `\"lock\": false`: Deno finds `package.json` only next to `deno.json`, and\nthe lock it would write for this config would replace `deno.lock`.\n\n`REQUIRE_GPU=1` turns a missing adapter into a failure:\n`tests/helpers/gpu.js` throws\n`REQUIRE_GPU=1 but this runtime has no WebGPU adapter` and the runner exits\nwith 1 and prints `suite gpu needs Deno on PATH` when Deno is missing. The\nworkflow sets it for the suites `gpu` and `all`.\n\nOn Linux without a GPU, Deno's WebGPU falls back to Mesa's software OpenGL ES\ndriver; install it with\n\n```bash\nsudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libegl1 libgles2 libegl-mesa0 libgl1-mesa-dri\ndeno run -A scripts/gpu-adapter.mjs   # prints the adapter, or null\nREQUIRE_GPU=1 npm run test:heavy -- --suite gpu\n```\n\nEvery GPU test prints its adapter (`WebGPU adapter: {...}`) and the report\n`gpu-solver.md` names it. A software adapter says nothing about GPU speed.\n\n### Recognition benchmark\n\nRun a short sample locally or dispatch the full recognition suite on one\nGitHub Actions runner core:\n\n```bash\nnode scripts/run-heavy.mjs --suite recognition --limit 5\ngh workflow run heavy.yml -f suite=recognition\n```\n\nThe benchmark uses the first rows of each set in\n[datasets/benchmark.json](../datasets/benchmark.json). Keep fetched audio and\ntranscripts in `.datasets/`. Only the aggregate Markdown report and a JSON\nreport with aggregate counts and rates and per-row IDs and counts go into the\nworkflow artifact. Use the default prefixes for comparisons against the\ncommitted baseline. The recognition workflow has a 90-minute test budget.\n\nTo set or update the baseline, run the full suite on comparable single-core\nhardware:\n\n```bash\nHEAVY_UPDATE_BASELINE=1 node scripts/run-heavy.mjs --suite recognition\n```\n\nOnce all benchmark corpora are measured and pass the floors, this writes\n`tests/heavy/baselines/recognition.json` and\n`docs/reports/recognition-benchmark.md`. Review and commit both files. An update\nthat raises an error rate requires `HEAVY_BASELINE_REASON=\"...\"`, which is stored\nwith the new baseline. A regular run with the same limits and utterance counts\nallows two percentage points of error increase, four points of language\naccuracy loss, and up to 1.5 times the baseline real-time factor.\n\n### Policy check\n\nThe [vision](VISION.md) rules out neural networks and asks for a result in\nthe public domain. `npm run check:policy` (part of `npm run check` and of the\nCI job \"Lint and Format Check\") enforces both by machine. It uses Node.js\nbuilt-ins only, so it also runs before `npm install`. What counts as a neural\nnetwork is described in\n[What counts as a neural network](VISION.md#what-counts-as-a-neural-network);\nthe lists the check uses are in `scripts/policy-denylist.json`.\n\nWhat is checked, in every file that `git ls-files` lists:\n\n- **Dependencies** (`package`): the names in every `package.json`\n  (`dependencies`, `devDependencies`, `optionalDependencies`,\n  `peerDependencies`), every `package-lock.json`, `deno.lock`, the import map\n  of `deno.json`, `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`, `requirements*.txt` and\n  `pyproject.toml` are compared with\n  `deniedPackages` (npm, cargo and python). A pattern is an exact name or a\n  prefix that ends with `*`; Rust and Python names treat `-` and `_` alike.\n- **Imports** (`package`): in `.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.jsx`, `.ts`, `.tsx`,\n  `.html`, `.rs`, `.py`, `.sh`, `.yml`, `.yaml` files and in `Dockerfile`, a\n  denied name in `from '...'`, `import('...')`, `require('...')`,\n  `use <crate>::`, `extern crate`, Python `import` / `from ... import`, a CDN\n  URL (`.../npm/<name>`, `/<name>@<version>`), or after an install command\n  such as `npm install`, `npx`, `bunx`, `pip install` or `cargo add`.\n- **Model files** (`file`): a file name that ends with one of\n  `deniedFileExtensions` (`.onnx`, `.pt`, `.safetensors`, `.gguf`, ...), in\n  any case.\n- **Licences** (`licence`): the `license` of every package in every npm lock\n  file, and of every crate in `cargo metadata` when there is a `Cargo.toml` at\n  the root, must pass `allowedLicences`. `A OR B` passes when one side passes,\n  `A AND B` when both do; a missing licence fails.\n- **Datasets** (`dataset`): every error that `validateRegistry` of\n  `scripts/datasets.mjs` finds in `datasets/registry.json` (see\n  [Datasets](#datasets)), including a licence that is not in\n  `allowedDatasetLicences`, and every tracked file under `.datasets/`. These\n  findings cannot be excepted.\n- **Lexicon sources** (`lexicon`): `lexiconSources(root, list)` reports every\n  entry of `data/lexicon/sources.json` (the sources of the shipped\n  pronunciation lexicons) whose `licence` does not pass `allowedLicences`,\n  whose `licenceQuote` is empty, that has no `licenceChecked` date or whose\n  `url` or file URL lies under a URL of `data/lexicon/refused.json`\n  (CC-CEDICT, OpenRussian, Wiktionary and other share-alike, non-commercial\n  or unclear sources). These findings cannot be excepted either; add a\n  source's licence text and copyright line to `src/g2p/lexicon/NOTICE.md`.\n\nWords are not checked: `docs/`, `dev/log/`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `.changeset/`,\nthe list itself and its test are skipped, and \"neural\" may be written\nanywhere.\n\nA finding is printed as `file:line rule name: message`, for example:\n\n```text\npackage.json:4 package onnxruntime-node: depends on the denied npm package (pattern \"onnxruntime-*\")\n```\n\nIt means: line 4 of `package.json` names the package `onnxruntime-node`,\nwhich matches the npm pattern `onnxruntime-*`. Remove the dependency, the\nimport or the file, or choose a package with a permissive licence. Without a\nfinding the check prints `policy: ok (N packages, M files)`; with `--json` it\nprints the findings as JSON, and `--root <dir>` checks another repository.\n\nAn exception is an entry\n`{\"rule\": \"package\" | \"file\" | \"licence\", \"match\": \"<package name or file path>\", \"reason\": \"<sentence>\"}`\nin `exceptions`. It needs a non-empty reason and the approval of the\nrepository owner in the pull request that adds it. An exception that matches\nnothing is itself a finding (rule `exception`), so stale exceptions are\nremoved.\n\n### Datasets\n\nTests that need real speech take it from the datasets listed in\n[datasets/registry.json](../datasets/registry.json). Only that list is\ncommitted; `npm run datasets` (`scripts/datasets.mjs`, Node.js built-ins\nonly) downloads a small part of a dataset into `.datasets/<id>/`, which git\nignores, and checks it against the SHA-256 in the list.\n\n```bash\nnpm run datasets -- list                 # id, languages, licence, kind, cached or not\nnpm run datasets -- fetch fleurs-ru --limit 3\nnpm run datasets -- verify               # the registry, and the cache without the network\n```\n\n`fetch` prints one line per file (`cached`, `downloaded` or `resumed` and\nthe byte count) and fetches a cached file with the right checksum only once.\nOptions: `--cache <dir>` (default `.datasets`), `--limit <n>` (kind `rows`:\nthe audio of the first `n` rows, default 20), `--max-bytes <n>` (refuse a\nlarger download, default 209715200) and `--record`. Exit codes: 0 ok, 2 wrong\nusage or unknown id, 3 licence refused, 4 checksum or size mismatch, 5 too\nlarge, 6 network failure. A download is resumed from `<file>.part` with a\nrange request; a failed request is tried up to 4 times, waiting 2, 4 and 6\nseconds between the attempts.\n\nEvery dataset belongs to one of three classes:\n\n1. **May be committed**: licence `Public-Domain` or `CC0-1.0` and no extra\n   terms; the entry has `\"redistribution\": true`. A part of it may be added\n   to the repository by the issue that needs it, never the whole cache.\n2. **Fetch only**: any other licence of `allowedDatasetLicences` in\n   `scripts/policy-denylist.json` (`CC-BY-4.0`, `CC-BY-3.0`, `Apache-2.0`,\n   `MIT`, `BSD-2-Clause`, `BSD-3-Clause`, `Unicode-3.0`,\n   `Custom-Attribution`); the entry has\n   `\"redistribution\": false`. Tests download it at run time.\n3. **Refused**: everything else (non-commercial, no-derivatives, share-alike,\n   GPL, paid, behind a login, re-hosting forbidden, unknown). Well-known\n   examples are listed with the reason in\n   [datasets/refused.json](../datasets/refused.json); a registry entry that\n   names one of their URLs is an error. The licence gate has no switch.\n\nTo add an entry:\n\n1. Read the licence page and copy the sentence that grants the licence into\n   `licenceQuote`, its address into `licenceUrl` and the day into\n   `licenceChecked` (`YYYY-MM-DD`). `licence` is an SPDX identifier,\n   `Public-Domain` or `Custom-Attribution`.\n2. Fill in `id` (lower case letters, digits and `-`), `title`, `languages`\n   (`en`, `ru`, `hi`, `zh`), `redistribution`, `citation` and `source`: kind\n   `files` (a list of `name`, `url`, `size`, `sha256` and an optional\n   `transcripts`, the name of the file with the text) or kind `rows` (the\n   Hugging Face rows interface: `dataset`, `config`, `split`, `length` of at\n   most 100, `textColumn`, `textSha256`). URLs are `https://`.\n3. Never invent a checksum: write `null`, run\n   `npm run datasets -- fetch <id> --record`, which downloads the data and\n   writes the size and the SHA-256 into the registry, and commit the result.\n   `textSha256` of kind `rows` is the SHA-256 of the texts of the rows joined\n   with `\\n`; it pins the revision, so a changed dataset fails with exit 4.\n4. `npm run datasets -- verify` and `npm run check:policy` must pass.\n\nFetched audio and text never enter the repository, a release or an\nartifact: `.datasets/` is ignored, `npm run check:policy` reports a tracked\nfile under it, and `fetch` writes `ATTRIBUTION.txt` (title, licence, licence\nsource and citation) next to the data. The workflow `Heavy checks` keeps\n`.datasets` in the GitHub Actions cache under the key\n`datasets-<hash of datasets/registry.json>`, so a changed registry fetches\nagain.\n\nIn a test, `datasetSkipReason(id)` of `tests/helpers/datasets.js` returns\n`null` when the dataset is in the cache and verifies, otherwise the reason\nwhy its first URL cannot be reached (or `null` when it can); pass it to\n`itUnless`, then call `fetchDataset(id)` and `readDataset(id)`, which returns\n`{id, text, audioPath, gender}` for every cached recording.\n\n### Golden set\n\n[tests/fixtures/golden/](../tests/fixtures/golden/README.md) holds 24 short\nsentences from public-domain LibriVox recordings, 6 each in English,\nRussian, Hindi and Mandarin, with their text and hand-written IPA. Tests\nread them without the network through `loadGolden({ lang, reviewedOnly })`\nof `tests/helpers/golden.js`. The fixtures README describes how a file is\nmade with `node scripts/golden.mjs pauses` and `cut`. After any change,\n`node scripts/golden.mjs verify` must print nothing and exit 0. It checks:\n\n- the manifest;\n- the SHA-256 of every file;\n- the format (16 kHz, mono, 16-bit FLAC);\n- the total size (at most 2 000 000 bytes);\n- that every source is a `redistribution: true` entry of the registry;\n- the rate of speech;\n- the IPA.\n\nOnly a person who listened to a file may set its `review.text` and\n`review.ipa` to `confirmed` and `review.by` to their GitHub name; an\nautomatic agent never does.\n\n### Listening tests\n\nA blind listening test with\n[examples/listening-test/](../examples/listening-test/README.md) is required\nbefore a claim about naturalness is written anywhere: in the README, a\nrelease note, a pull request or a report. The steps for organising one are\nin that README; in short:\n\n1. Write a sentences file (`sentences.example.json` shows one trial of each\n   kind; `node scripts/listening-test.mjs sus --lang en --count 20 --seed 1`\n   writes sentences for intelligibility trials).\n2. `node scripts/listening-test.mjs build --sentences <file.json> --out examples/listening-test`\n   writes `stimuli/` and `config.js`, which are not committed.\n3. Send the folder to at least 8 listeners. With fewer, the report says that\n   its numbers support no claim, and no claim may be based on it.\n4. `node scripts/listening-test.mjs analyze <result.json>... --out docs/reports/listening/<test id>/report.md`.\n   Commit the result files and the report to\n   `docs/reports/listening/<test id>/`.\n\nThe start screen shows this consent sentence, and only results of\nlisteners who pressed \"Start\" after reading it are published: \"Your answers\nare saved in a file on this computer only. It holds your ratings, the time\nyou spent on each trial, whether you use headphones and, if you give it,\nyour native language; it holds no name, address or browser details. By\npressing \"Start\" you agree that this file may be published as part of the\nresults of the test.\"\n\nAudio of other synthesisers enters a test only through `extra` in the\nsentences file. It is never committed and no code in this repository runs\nanother synthesiser.\n\n### Rust engine\n\nA new engine feature is one entry in `ENGINE_FEATURES`, one line in\n`features.rs` and one parity probe; the check fails otherwise.\n`node scripts/check-engine-parity.mjs` runs in `npm run check` and Rust CI.\nEvery acoustics module belongs to a feature or to `JS_ONLY` with a reason.\nRun `node scripts/check-engine-parity.mjs --write-vectors` after porting a\nfeature to regenerate its JavaScript reference vector. With built wasm,\n`REQUIRE_WASM=1 node --test tests/engine-parity.test.js` must pass with zero\nhandoffs. The heavy performance suite measures every feature and every tier\nfor at least two seconds per engine; copy `engine-parity.md` from its green\nartifact to `docs/reports/engine-parity.md`, alongside the performance trend.\n\nThe Rust workspace in `crates/` reproduces numerical code of `src/` as one\nWebAssembly file. [RUST-ENGINE.md](RUST-ENGINE.md) has the interface rules,\nthe determinism rules and the parity classes; read it before porting code.\nIn short:\n\n1. `rustup toolchain install` installs the compiler pinned in\n   `rust-toolchain.toml`; `npm run build:wasm` builds\n   `src/engine/voice-simulator.wasm`, which is git-ignored.\n2. Before a pull request, run `cargo fmt --all --check`,\n   `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings`,\n   `cargo test --workspace --locked` and\n   `REQUIRE_WASM=1 node --test tests/rust-parity.test.js`.\n3. A new crate is added to `scripts/rust-allowed-crates.json` with its\n   licence in the same pull request; only permissive licences are allowed.\n\nWithout `cargo` everything else still works: the build script prints a note\nand the parity tests are skipped with their reason.\n\n## Version Management with Changesets\n\nThis project uses [Changesets](https://github.com/changesets/changesets) to manage versions and changelogs. This eliminates merge conflicts that occur when multiple PRs bump the version in `package.json`.\n\n### Adding a Changeset\n\nWhen you make changes that affect users, add a changeset:\n\n```bash\nbun run changeset\n# or\nnpm run changeset\n```\n\nThis will prompt you to:\n\n1. Select the type of change (patch/minor/major)\n2. Provide a summary of the changes\n\nThe changeset will be saved as a markdown file in `.changeset/` and should be committed with your PR.\n\n### Changeset Guidelines\n\n| Type      | When to Use                          | Examples                                            |\n| --------- | ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------- |\n| **Patch** | Bug fixes, internal changes          | Fix typo, update dependency, refactor internal code |\n| **Minor** | New features, non-breaking additions | Add new function, new optional parameter            |\n| **Major** | Breaking changes                     | Remove function, change API signature               |\n\nExample changeset summary:\n\n```markdown\nAdd support for custom configuration via config file\n```\n\n### What Changes Need Changesets?\n\n**Required** for:\n\n- Bug fixes\n- New features\n- Breaking changes\n- Public API changes\n\n**Not required** for:\n\n- Documentation-only changes (in `./docs` folder)\n- Changes to markdown files\n- CI/CD workflow updates (unless they affect users)\n\n### PR guard comparison and local validation\n\nVersion and changeset guards compare the PR head with its merge base. CI passes\n`GITHUB_BASE_SHA` and `GITHUB_HEAD_SHA`; local runs default to `origin/main` and\n`HEAD`. Fetch the base before running the guards. Missing refs, Git failures,\nand invalid package metadata fail validation.\n\nThe changeset guard counts added fragments only. Exact file moves do not count\nas new fragments; replacing a deleted fragment with different content does.\nBoth paths of a move are checked when deciding whether code requires a fragment.\nMarkdown, `docs/`, `examples/`,\n`experiments/`, `dev/log/`, and changeset metadata are exempt. In multi-language\nrepositories, unrelated language roots are exempt; shared workflows still\nrequire a fragment. For local directory validation without Git comparison, use\n`ALLOW_LOCAL_CHANGESET_SCAN=true node scripts/validate-changeset.mjs`. This\nexplicit mode is forbidden in CI. Set `DEBUG=1` to print comparison details.\n\nAutomated release PRs are exempt only when their author matches the release\nactor, both repositories match `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`, and their branch uses a\nrelease prefix. The default author is `github-actions[bot]`. When a dedicated\nrelease token creates PRs as another account, configure repository variable\n`RELEASE_PR_ACTOR` to that account's exact login. A branch name alone never\ngrants an exemption.\n\n## Release Process\n\nThe release process is fully automated:\n\n1. **PR with changeset merged** - The changeset is added to `.changeset/`\n2. **CI detects changesets** - On push to main, CI checks for pending changesets\n3. **Version bump** - Package version is updated based on changeset type\n4. **Changelog update** - `CHANGELOG.md` is updated automatically\n5. **npm publish** - Package is published via OIDC trusted publishing\n6. **GitHub Release** - A release is created with formatted notes\n\nChangesets explicitly uses Prettier in `.changeset/config.json`, matching\n`format:check`. Keep that setting when adding runtime configs: auto-detection\nselects Deno for any `deno.json`, independently of the npm package-manager\ndeclaration. PR lint checks dry-run `npm run changeset:version` after the fresh\nmerge simulation and restore the generated metadata and consumed fragments.\nThis requires no publishing credentials and runs independently of release\ncredential preflight.\n\n### Multiple Changesets\n\nIf multiple PRs are merged before a release:\n\n- All changesets are merged into one\n- The highest version bump type wins (major > minor > patch)\n- All descriptions are preserved in chronological order\n\n## Pull Request Guidelines\n\n### PR Title\n\nUse a clear, descriptive title that summarizes the change:\n\n```\nfeat: Add support for custom configuration\nfix: Resolve race condition in async handler\ndocs: Update API documentation for v2\n```\n\n### PR Description\n\nInclude:\n\n- **What** - Describe the change\n- **Why** - Explain the motivation\n- **Testing** - How the change was tested\n\n### CI Checks\n\nAll PRs must pass:\n\n- [ ] Test compilation (syntax check)\n- [ ] Lint, format, and secrets scan\n- [ ] File line limits check\n- [ ] Changeset validation (for code changes)\n- [ ] Documentation validation (when docs change)\n- [ ] Ubuntu tests on Node.js, Bun, and Deno\n\n### Fresh Merge Simulation\n\nThe CI workflow automatically:\n\n1. Merges the latest `main` into your PR branch\n2. Runs checks against the merged state\n\nIf this fails with merge conflicts, you need to:\n\n```bash\ngit fetch origin main\ngit merge origin/main\n# Resolve conflicts\ngit push\n```\n\n## Questions?\n\nIf you have questions about contributing, feel free to open an issue for discussion.\n\n## Case Studies\n\nCase studies of this repository live in `docs/case-studies/issue-N` where N is the number of the issue in this repository.\nFolders named `template-issue-N` were inherited from the template repository and are kept for reference only; see the [index of case studies](case-studies/README.md).\n\n## Auto-regenerated preview screenshots\n\nThe `example-app.yml` workflow contains a `preview-regen` job that boots\nthe built example app in a headless Chromium via\n[`browser-commander`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/browser-commander) +\nPlaywright and writes fresh screenshots to\n`docs/screenshots/example-app/example-app-{locale}-{theme}.png` on every\npush to `main` (and on `workflow_dispatch`). [2026-11-22T13:03:02.459Z] [STDERR] # Vision
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.477Z] [STDERR] voice-simulator is a physical model of the human voice that works in both
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.501Z] [STDERR] directions:
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.505Z] [STDERR] ```
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.507Z] [STDERR] text in a language  ->  IPA  ->  articulation  ->  sound      (speaking)
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.509Z] [STDERR] text in a language  <-  IPA  <-  articulation  <-  sound      (listening)
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.510Z] [STDERR] ```
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.522Z] [STDERR] Speaking simulates the air in a human head. Listening runs the same simulation
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.529Z] [STDERR] in reverse: it finds the head, the voice and the movements that would have
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.538Z] [STDERR] produced the sound it hears, and reads the speech off those movements. Nothing
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.564Z] [STDERR] is recorded and nothing is learned by a neural network. The project is in the
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.580Z] [STDERR] public domain and is a gift to everyone.
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.597Z] [STDERR] This document is the single statement of where the project is going. It is
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.607Z] [STDERR] updated by every pull request that changes the direction; the history is at the
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.609Z] [STDERR] end. The step-by-step plan that implements it is [ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md).
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.620Z] [STDERR] ## Principles
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.628Z] [STDERR] These are rules, not preferences. A change that breaks one of them is not
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.637Z] [STDERR] merged.
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.646Z] [STDERR] 1. **Physics and mathematics only.** Sound comes from simulated air, folds,
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.655Z] [STDERR]    walls and turbulence. Recognition comes from inverting that simulation.
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.671Z] [STDERR]    No neural network is used anywhere: not in the library, not in the app,
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.678Z] [STDERR]    not in the tests and not in the tools that build the data tables. No
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.682Z] [STDERR]    recorded speech is played back or concatenated. The exact boundary is in
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.686Z] [STDERR]    [What counts as a neural network](#what-counts-as-a-neural-network).
[2026-11-22T13:03:02.697Z] [STDERR] 2. **One model, two directions.** Speak

It returns a copy of `result` (shape of `recognize`) with `modes` and `ipa` filled in.\n\n1. Span shape, as in #70: the shape of `plan.modes` of #50 plus four keys. Example:\n\n   ```text\n   { start: 0.4, end: 1.9, from: 1, to: 5, effort: 0.75,\n     notation: 'f', confidence: 0.8 }\n   ```\n\n   `start`, `end` in seconds; `from`, `to` are indexes into `result.words` (`to` exclusive); then only the decided keys of the mode object of #50; `notation` is the brace label or `null` when IPA has none (emotion); `confidence` is 0 to 1.\n\n2. Baseline: what this speaker sounds like in a normal voice.\n   - With `options.voice` (a voice of #41 or #63): synthesise `tests/fixtures/recognition/baseline.txt` (one neutral sentence per language, write it here) with that voice at the tier that matches `sampleRate` and measure the features of step 3. Cache by voice.\n   - Without it: the median of each feature over the utterance. Then only changes inside the utterance and the signs that need no baseline (whisper, creak, falsetto) can be reported. Do not guess the rest.\n3. Features per word, from the frames of its vowels (`analyzeFrames`, `trackPitch`, `trackFormants`, `inverseFilter`, `mode-features.js`): `alpha` (alpha ratio, dB), `pitch` (median, Hz and semitones re the baseline), `f1` (mean F1 minus the baseline F1 of the same vowel, Hz; `null` without `options.voice`), `voiced` (voiced share of the vowel frames), `h1h2` (corrected for formants, dB), `hnr` (dB), `cpp` (dB), `jitter` (%), `rate` (syllables per second of the word and its two neighbours). `d` before a name below means \"minus the baseline\".\n4. Effort in decibels (inverse of `EFFORT_RULES` of #52): `Etilt = dalpha / 0.2`, `Epitch = dpitch in Hz / 5`, `Ef1 = df1 / 3.5`; `E = 0.6 * Etilt + 0.2 * Epitch + 0.2 * Ef1` (without `f1`: 0.75 and 0.25); `effort = clamp(0.5 + E / 40, 0, 1)`, rounded to the nearest of 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1. `confidence = max(0, 1 - |Etilt - Epitch| / 20)`.\n5. Label per word, first rule that fits (start values; tune with the tests):\n\n   | Rule | Keys | Label |\n   | --- | --- | --- |\n   | `voiced < 0.05` and energy ratio 6 dB above the baseline | `phonation.whisper: 1` | `W` |\n   | median pitch below 70 Hz | `phonation.creaky: 1` | `C` |\n   | `dpitch >= 10` st and `h1h2 >= 8` | `phonation.falsetto: 1` | `F` |\n   | `h1h2 < 0`, `dhnr <= -3`, `jitter >= 3` | `phonation.harsh: 1` | `V!` |\n   | `jitter >= 5`, and `h1h2 < 0` or `dpitch <= -8` st | `phonation.creaky` | `V̰` |\n   | `dh1h2 <= -3` and `dhnr >= -2` | `phonation.tension: 1` | `V͈` |\n   | `dh1h2 >= 1` and (`dcpp <= -1` or `dhnr <= -3`) | `phonation.breathy` | `V̤` |\n   | voiced, `hnr < 10`, `dhnr <= -4` | `phonation.whisper: 0.5` | `Ṿ` |\n   | `dh1h2` between 2 and 5, `dhnr` between -2 and 2 | `phonation.tension: -1` | `V͉` |\n   | `effort` of step 4 is not 0.5 and no row above fits | `effort` | `pp`, `p`, `f`, `ff` |\n   | `rate / baseline rate >= 1.2` (may be added to any row) | `rate: 1.3` | `allegro` |\n   | `rate / baseline rate <= 0.83` (may be added to any row) | `rate: 0.75` | `lento` |\n\n   Degree of breathy and creaky voice: `d = clamp(dh1h2 / 3.2, 0, 1)` (breathy) or `clamp(jitter / 5, 0, 1)` (creaky), rounded to 0.33, 0.67 or 1 and written as `{1V̤`, `{V̤`, `{3V̤`. Use the key names and signs that #54 really has; this table uses those of #50.\n\n6. From words to spans: join neighbouring words with the same label. One word between two words with the same label takes their label. A span shorter than 0.3 s is dropped, except whisper. Inside a span of 4 words or more with a label of effort, fit a line to `E` over time: a change of 8 dB or more gives `crescendo` (rising) or `diminuendo` instead.\n7. Whisper spans: use `findWhisper` of `src/recognition/whisper.js` when that file exists (#72); otherwise the first row of the table.\n8. Emotion, per phrase (words between pauses of 0.2 s or more):\n   1. Vector: pitch level (st), pitch span (95th minus 5th percentile, st), `rate` ratio, `E`, `dh1h2`, `dhnr`; each minus the baseline and divided by its scale: 2 st, 2 st, 0.15, 5 dB, 3 dB, 3 dB.\n   2. Reference vectors: on first use, synthesise the baseline sentence once per emotion name of #55 at intensity 1 with the baseline voice and measure the same vector. No trained model is used.\n   3. `activation` = mean of the first four components divided by 2, cut to -1…1. Always reported when `|activation| >= 0.3`, as `emotion: { arousal: activation }`.\n   4. Name: the nearest reference by Euclidean distance `near`; `next` is the second nearest. Report `emotion.name` only when `near <= 0.6 * (length of the vector)` and `near <= 0.8 * next`; `intensity` = length of the vector divided by the length of the reference, cut to 0…1; `confidence = 1 - near / next`.\n   5. When a name is reported, drop the effort, rate and phonation spans of that phrase which the emotion preset of #55 itself produces (same key, value within one step), so that speaking the result again does not apply them twice. `notation` is `null`.\n9. Sounds, only when #56 is merged: a noise of 0.3 to 0.7 s inside a pause is `⸨inhale⸩`; 3 or more bursts of voice at 4 to 6 per second are `⸨laugh⸩`; a steady `ə`-like vowel longer than 0.2 s next to a pause is `⸨filler⸩`. Add the token to `ipa`, and to `modes` a span `{ start, end, sound, notation, confidence }`.\n10. Write `ipa`: wrap the words of every span that has a label in `{label … label}`, with `formatIpa` of #50. Export `toPlanModes(modes)`: it returns `[{ from, to, mode }]` for `planUtterance(ipa, { modes })`, including the spans without a label.\n11. What cannot be decided is left out. The answer is a list of spans in `result.modes` and the same ExtIPA/VoQS brace marks in `result.ipa` that the synthesiser reads (`{f … f}`, `{W … W}`, `{V̤ … V̤}`), so that speaking the result again gives the same manner of speech.\n\n## Why\n\nThe issue asks for volume, whisper, emotions and \"all common modes of speech\" for input as well as output. #52 to #55 make the synthesiser speak these modes; each of them lists the measurable signs of its mode. This issue reads those signs back. Copying a recording (#79) needs them.\n\n## Current state\n\n- After #73, `recognize` returns `modes: []`. #70 (if merged) adds spans for emphasis and sentence tunes and fixes the span shape.\n- `analyzeVoice` in `src/analysis/voice-features.js` gives one value per recording for `f0`, `h1h2`, `hnr` and others. It gives nothing over time.\n- After #52, #53 and #54, `src/analysis/mode-features.js` has `levelDb`, `alphaRatio`, `voicedShare`, `energyRatio`, `centreOfGravity`, `cpp` and `jitterPercent`, and each of those issues has a table \"How the mode is written and recognised\" with target values. After #61, `inverseFilter` gives the measures of the voice source per frame.\n- The absolute level of a recording says nothing about effort: it depends on the microphone and its distance. The research notes (file 4) give the usable signs: [REDACTED]\n- Emotion: the same notes say that activation (calm or excited) can be heard from prosody, that people name one of 7 emotions from prosody alone about 58 % right (Pell et al. 2009), and that pleasant or unpleasant is hard to hear. No public-domain recordings of emotions or whisper exist.\n\n## What to do\n\nCreate `src/recognition/modes.js` exporting `recognizeModes(samples, sampleRate, result, options)`. It returns a copy of `result` (shape of `recognize`) with `modes` and `ipa` filled in.\n\n1. Span shape, as in #70: the shape of `plan.modes` of #50 plus four keys. Example:\n\n   ```text\n   { start: 0.4, end: 1.9, from: 1, to: 5, effort: 0.75,\n     notation: 'f', confidence: 0.8 }\n   ```\n\n   `start`, `end` in seconds; `from`, `to` are indexes into `result.words` (`to` exclusive); then only the decided keys of the mode object of #50; `notation` is the brace label or `null` when IPA has none (emotion); `confidence` is 0 to 1.\n\n2. Baseline: what this speaker sounds like in a normal voice.\n   - With `options.voice` (a voice of #41 or #63): synthesise `tests/fixtures/recognition/baseline.txt` (one neutral sentence per language, write it here) with that voice at the tier that matches `sampleRate` and measure the features of step 3. Cache by voice.\n   - Without it: the median of each feature over the utterance. Then only changes inside the utterance and the signs that need no baseline (whisper, creak, falsetto) can be reported. Do not guess the rest.\n3. Features per word, from the frames of its vowels (`analyzeFrames`, `trackPitch`, `trackFormants`, `inverseFilter`, `mode-features.js`): `alpha` (alpha ratio, dB), `pitch` (median, Hz and semitones re the baseline), `f1` (mean F1 minus the baseline F1 of the same vowel, Hz; `null` without `options.voice`), `voiced` (voiced share of the vowel frames), `h1h2` (corrected for formants, dB), `hnr` (dB), `cpp` (dB), `jitter` (%), `rate` (syllables per second of the word and its two neighbours). `d` before a name below means \"minus the baseline\".\n4. Effort in decibels (inverse of `EFFORT_RULES` of #52): `Etilt = dalpha / 0.2`, `Epitch = dpitch in Hz / 5`, `Ef1 = df1 / 3.5`; `E = 0.6 * Etilt + 0.2 * Epitch + 0.2 * Ef1` (without `f1`: 0.75 and 0.25); `effort = clamp(0.5 + E / 40, 0, 1)`, rounded to the nearest of 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1. `confidence = max(0, 1 - |Etilt - Epitch| / 20)`.\n5. Label per word, first rule that fits (start values; tune with the tests):\n\n   | Rule | Keys | Label |\n   | --- | --- | --- |\n   | `voiced < 0.05` and energy ratio 6 dB above the baseline | `phonation.whisper: 1` | `W` |\n   | median pitch below 70 Hz | `phonation.creaky: 1` | `C` |\n   | `dpitch >= 10` st and `h1h2 >= 8` | `phonation.falsetto: 1` | `F` |\n   | `h1h2 < 0`, `dhnr <= -3`, `jitter >= 3` | `phonation.harsh: 1` | `V!` |\n   | `jitter >= 5`, and `h1h2 < 0` or `dpitch <= -8` st | `phonation.creaky` | `V̰` |\n   | `dh1h2 <= -3` and `dhnr >= -2` | `phonation.tension: 1` | `V͈` |\n   | `dh1h2 >= 1` and (`dcpp <= -1` or `dhnr <= -3`) | `phonation.breathy` | `V̤` |\n   | voiced, `hnr < 10`, `dhnr <= -4` | `phonation.whisper: 0.5` | `Ṿ` |\n   | `dh1h2` between 2 and 5, `dhnr` between -2 and 2 | `phonation.tension: -1` | `V͉` |\n   | `effort` of step 4 is not 0.5 and no row above fits | `effort` | `pp`, `p`, `f`, `ff` |\n   | `rate / baseline rate >= 1.2` (may be added to any row) | `rate: 1.3` | `allegro` |\n   | `rate / baseline rate <= 0.83` (may be added to any row) | `rate: 0.75` | `lento` |\n\n   Degree of breathy and creaky voice: `d = clamp(dh1h2 / 3.2, 0, 1)` (breathy) or `clamp(jitter / 5, 0, 1)` (creaky), rounded to 0.33, 0.67 or 1 and written as `{1V̤`, `{V̤`, `{3V̤`. Use the key names and signs that #54 really has; this table uses those of #50.\n\n6. From words to spans: join neighbouring words with the same label. One word between two words with the same label takes their label. A span shorter than 0.3 s is dropped, except whisper. Inside a span of 4 words or more with a label of effort, fit a line to `E` over time: a change of 8 dB or more gives `crescendo` (rising) or `diminuendo` instead.\n7. Whisper spans: use `findWhisper` of `src/recognition/whisper.js` when that file exists (#72); otherwise the first row of the table.\n8. Emotion, per phrase (words between pauses of 0.2 s or more):\n   1. Vector: pitch level (st), pitch span (95th minus 5th percentile, st), `rate` ratio, `E`, `dh1h2`, `dhnr`; each minus the baseline and divided by its scale: 2 st, 2 st, 0.15, 5 dB, 3 dB, 3 dB.\n   2. Reference vectors: on first use, synthesise the baseline sentence once per emotion name of #55 at intensity 1 with the baseline voice and measure the same vector. No trained model is used.\n   3. `activation` = mean of the first four components divided by 2, cut to -1…1. Always reported when `|activation| >= 0.3`, as `emotion: { arousal: activation }`.\n   4. Name: the nearest reference by Euclidean distance `near`; `next` is the second nearest. Report `emotion.name` only when `near <= 0.6 * (length of the vector)` and `near <= 0.8 * next`; `intensity` = length of the vector divided by the length of the reference, cut to 0…1; `confidence = 1 - near / next`.\n   5. When a name is reported, drop the effort, rate and phonation spans of that phrase which the emotion preset of #55 itself produces (same key, value within one step), so that speaking the result again does not apply them twice. `notation` is `null`.\n9. Sounds, only when #56 is merged: a noise of 0.3 to 0.7 s inside a pause is `⸨inhale⸩`; 3 or more bursts of voice at 4 to 6 per second are `⸨laugh⸩`; a steady `ə`-like vowel longer than 0.2 s next to a pause is `⸨filler⸩`. Add the token to `ipa`, and to `modes` a span `{ start, end, sound, notation, confidence }`.\n10. Write `ipa`: wrap the words of every span that has a label in `{label … label}`, with `formatIpa` of #50. Export `toPlanModes(modes)`: it returns `[{ from, to, mode }]` for `planUtterance(ipa, { modes })`, including the spans without a label.\n11. What cannot be decided is left out. Never report an emotion name, an effort or a voice quality for a phrase with fewer than 3 vowels.\n12. Wiring: if `src/recognition/recognizer.js` exists, call `recognizeModes` after the text step when the option `modes` is not `false`, and pass the option `voice` on; otherwise #73 adds the call. In `tests/heavy/roundtrip-*.test.js` of #75, if merged, add the gates of the acceptance criteria. Export from `src/index.js`, add types, and describe the span shape in `README.md`.\n\n## Tests\n\n`tests/recognition-modes.test.js`. Create `tests/helpers/roundtrip.js` exporting `roundTrip(text, options)` with `options = { lang, tier, preset, seed }`. Steps:\n   1. `spoken = synthesize(text, { lang, tier, preset, seed })`.\n   2. `heard = recognize(spoken.samples, spoken.sampleRate, { level })` with `level = levelForTier(tier)`. Do not pass the language: it must be found.\n   3. Return `{ spoken, heard, seconds }` plus these numbers, computed with `errorRate` and `editDistance` of #18:\n      - `per`: `errorRate(spoken.ipa, heard.ipa, 'phone')`;\n      - `wer` (not for `zh`) and `cer`: `errorRate(text, heard.text, unit)` with `'word'` and `'char'`;\n      - `soundWer`: the same as `wer`, but each word of both texts is first replaced by its IPA from `textToIpa(...).words[].ipa`, so that a word which sounds the same (`sea` and `see`, 他 and 她) is not an error. For `zh` the tokens are the characters;\n      - `toneErrors` (only `zh`): edit distance between the two lists of tones, one entry per syllable (the tone letters in the syllable's IPA, the empty string for the neutral tone);\n      - `stressHits` (only `en`, `ru`): among the reference words with two or more syllables whose recognised word has the same number of syllables, how many have `stress: 1` on the same syllable;\n      - `timeErrors`: pair the reference and recognised syllables through the edit-distance path over syllable IPA; for each pair with equal IPA collect `|start difference|` and `|end difference|` in ms;\n      - `languageRight`: `heard.languages[0].language === lang` after sorting by `share`, largest first;\n      - `sentenceMark`: the last of `. ? !` in `heard.text`, with `।`, `。`, `？`, `！` mapped to their ASCII form, or `null`.\n3. empty\n  means the branch picked)\n  and a `limit` (largest number of items, such as utterances or files, that\n  each test may process; empty means no limit);\n- from the command line:\n\n  ```bash\n  gh workflow run heavy.yml -f suite=quality -f limit=5\n  # on another branch\n  gh workflow run heavy.yml --ref my-branch -f suite=performance\n  ```\n\nA run started on `main` writes to the cache scope of `main`, so\n[scripts/resolve-heavy-ref.sh](../scripts/resolve-heavy-ref.sh) refuses a\n`ref` that names anything else, such as a commit of a fork; The answer is a list of spans in `result.modes` and the same ExtIPA/VoQS brace marks in `result.ipa` that the synthesiser reads (`{f … f}`, `{W … W}`, `{V̤ … V̤}`), so that speaking the result again gives the same manner of speech.\n\n## Why\n\nThe issue asks for volume, whisper, emotions and \"all common modes of speech\" for input as well as output. #52 to #55 make the synthesiser speak these modes; each of them lists the measurable signs of its mode. This issue reads those signs back. Copying a recording (#79) needs them.\n\n## Current state\n\n- After #73, `recognize` returns `modes: []`. #70 (if merged) adds spans for emphasis and sentence tunes and fixes the span shape.\n- `analyzeVoice` in `src/analysis/voice-features.js` gives one value per recording for `f0`, `h1h2`, `hnr` and others. It gives nothing over time.\n- After #52, #53 and #54, `src/analysis/mode-features.js` has `levelDb`, `alphaRatio`, `voicedShare`, `energyRatio`, `centreOfGravity`, `cpp` and `jitterPercent`, and each of those issues has a table \"How the mode is written and recognised\" with target values. After #61, `inverseFilter` gives the measures of the voice source per frame.\n- The absolute level of a recording says nothing about effort: it depends on the microphone and its distance. The research notes (file 4) give the usable signs: [REDACTED]\n- Emotion: the same notes say that activation (calm or excited) can be heard from prosody, that people name one of 7 emotions from prosody alone about 58 % right (Pell et al. 2009), and that pleasant or unpleasant is hard to hear. No public-domain recordings of emotions or whisper exist.\n\n## What to do\n\nCreate `src/recognition/modes.js` exporting `recognizeModes(samples, sampleRate, result, options)`. It returns a copy of `result` (shape of `recognize`) with `modes` and `ipa` filled in.\n\n1. Span shape, as in #70: the shape of `plan.modes` of #50 plus four keys. Example:\n\n   ```text\n   { start: 0.4, end: 1.9, from: 1, to: 5, effort: 0.75,\n     notation: 'f', confidence: 0.8 }\n   ```\n\n   `start`, `end` in seconds; `from`, `to` are indexes into `result.words` (`to` exclusive); then only the decided keys of the mode object of #50; `notation` is the brace label or `null` when IPA has none (emotion); `confidence` is 0 to 1.\n\n2. Baseline: what this speaker sounds like in a normal voice.\n   - With `options.voice` (a voice of #41 or #63): synthesise `tests/fixtures/recognition/baseline.txt` (one neutral sentence per language, write it here) with that voice at the tier that matches `sampleRate` and measure the features of step 3. Cache by voice.\n   - Without it: the median of each feature over the utterance. Then only changes inside the utterance and the signs that need no baseline (whisper, creak, falsetto) can be reported. Do not guess the rest.\n3. Features per word, from the frames of its vowels (`analyzeFrames`, `trackPitch`, `trackFormants`, `inverseFilter`, `mode-features.js`): `alpha` (alpha ratio, dB), `pitch` (median, Hz and semitones re the baseline), `f1` (mean F1 minus the baseline F1 of the same vowel, Hz; `null` without `options.voice`), `voiced` (voiced share of the vowel frames), `h1h2` (corrected for formants, dB), `hnr` (dB), `cpp` (dB), `jitter` (%), `rate` (syllables per second of the word and its two neighbours). `d` before a name below means \"minus the baseline\".\n4. Effort in decibels (inverse of `EFFORT_RULES` of #52): `Etilt = dalpha / 0.2`, `Epitch = dpitch in Hz / 5`, `Ef1 = df1 / 3.5`; `E = 0.6 * Etilt + 0.2 * Epitch + 0.2 * Ef1` (without `f1`: 0.75 and 0.25); `effort = clamp(0.5 + E / 40, 0, 1)`, rounded to the nearest of 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1. `confidence = max(0, 1 - |Etilt - Epitch| / 20)`.\n5. Label per word, first rule that fits (start values; tune with the tests):\n\n   | Rule | Keys | Label |\n   | --- | --- | --- |\n   | `voiced < 0.05` and energy ratio 6 dB above the baseline | `phonation.whisper: 1` | `W` |\n   | median pitch below 70 Hz | `phonation.creaky: 1` | `C` |\n   | `dpitch >= 10` st and `h1h2 >= 8` | `phonation.falsetto: 1` | `F` |\n   | `h1h2 < 0`, `dhnr <= -3`, `jitter >= 3` | `phonation.harsh: 1` | `V!` |\n   | `jitter >= 5`, and `h1h2 < 0` or `dpitch <= -8` st | `phonation.creaky` | `V̰` |\n   | `dh1h2 <= -3` and `dhnr >= -2` | `phonation.tension: 1` | `V͈` |\n   | `dh1h2 >= 1` and (`dcpp <= -1` or `dhnr <= -3`) | `phonation.breathy` | `V̤` |\n   | voiced, `hnr < 10`, `dhnr <= -4` | `phonation.whisper: 0.5` | `Ṿ` |\n   | `dh1h2` between 2 and 5, `dhnr` between -2 and 2 | `phonation.tension: -1` | `V͉` |\n   | `effort` of step 4 is not 0.5 and no row above fits | `effort` | `pp`, `p`, `f`, `ff` |\n   | `rate / baseline rate >= 1.2` (may be added to any row) | `rate: 1.3` | `allegro` |\n   | `rate / baseline rate <= 0.83` (may be added to any row) | `rate: 0.75` | `lento` |\n\n   Degree of breathy and creaky voice: `d = clamp(dh1h2 / 3.2, 0, 1)` (breathy) or `clamp(jitter / 5, 0, 1)` (creaky), rounded to 0.33, 0.67 or 1 and written as `{1V̤`, `{V̤`, `{3V̤`. Use the key names and signs that #54 really has; this table uses those of #50.\n\n6. From words to spans: join neighbouring words with the same label. One word between two words with the same label takes their label. A span shorter than 0.3 s is dropped, except whisper. Report `emotion.name` only when `near <= 0.6 * (length of the vector)` and `near <= 0.8 * next`; `intensity` = length of the vector divided by the length of the reference, cut to 0…1; `confidence = 1 - near / next`.\n   5.
